newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Chinese children sneak into Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chinese children sneak into Hong Kong.

text.p: Seven-year-old Mimi, one of 1,200 Chinese children soon to be deported to the mainland from Hong Kong as illegal immigrants, sat sobbing.
"All I want is an ID card and to stay with my daddy," she said.

The children are the latest protagonists in a long tragedy of migration from China, falling victim to the tough immigration rules of China and Hong Kong or families' impatience and disregard for the law.

The number of mainland Chinese children sneaking into Hong Kong has jumped this year, driven by rumours of an amnesty after China resumes control of the territory in July after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Hong Kong police arrested 1,367 young illegal Chinese migrants in the first quarter of 1997 against 90 in the year-earlier period.

While the Hong Kong government has repeatedly warned that all illegal immigrants will be sent packing back to China, some think that if they can stay in hiding until after the territory reverts to China, they will then be allowed to stay.
YOUNG ILLEGALS LIVE IN FEAR OF ARREST AND REPATRIATION
"I am afraid a policeman will pick me up. I want an ID card," said eight-year-old Chung Yuet-lam, who has overstayed a temporary permit and now faces possible deportation if caught.
Her mother, who has overstayed her permit to visit Hong Kong, said Yuet-lam should be allowed to stay.
"I can't accept this reality. Although she was smuggled in, she has the right to stay in Hong Kong. Her father is here. Her family is here. Basically she should be allowed to stay."
Yuet-lam is one of many children, born in China of Hong Kong fathers and mainland Chinese mothers, who have been smuggled into the territory in risky and expensive journeys.
Chinese parents now living legally in Hong Kong pay up to HK$3,000 (US$390) to have their children smuggled across the border or the sea into the capitalist "paradise" of Hong Kong.
"We have no choice," said a man who decided to smuggle his daughter from China into the territory, after trying for three years in vain to bribe Chinese officials for emigration papers.
A Chinese official told him it would take HK$30,000 (US$3,900) to get the job done, he said.
"If they won't let her get in legally, then our only alternative is to sneak her in," the man said helplessly.
When young illegals are caught in Hong Kong, their parents usually appeal against repatriation on humanitarian grounds.
Children are then issued with temporary papers allowing them to remain legally for prescribed periods, which can be extended.

Yuet-lam's recently expired. "I beg the Governor and the immigration director to consider letting her stay on grounds of compassion and human rights, so that she can continue her schooling here," her father said.
OFFICIAL CHANNELS CAN MEAN A LONG WAIT

Under Hong Kong's post-colonial constitution, known as the Basic Law, a person of Chinese nationality born outside Hong Kong will have right of abode here after the handover if, at the time of birth, one of his parents is a permanent resident.

Some 35,000 mainland children will have residency rights under such provisions. But under present rules, they must apply for immigration through official channels which can mean a long wait, especially because there is a daily quota of about 66 on the number of child immigrants Hong Kong will take from China.
Whether such children who cross the border illegally can stay after the handover will be up to the future Hong Kong government, immigration officials said.

Some sources say the new legislature that takes over on July 1 will bring in a law to ensure Chinese children who sneak into Hong Kong get sent back to the mainland, even if they qualify to come as legal permanent residents later.
Children are often smuggled to Hong Kong in flimsy old boats that may not be able to weather storms and big waves.
And they are easily caught. Two teenage illegal immigrants were recently found hiding in the Belgian Consul-General's home after sneaking successfully across the border.
Hong Kong police and Chinese authorities have been working together to try to solve the child smuggling problem.
PREGNANT WOMEN SNEAKING INTO HONG KONG

Pregnant mothers are also sneaking into the territory from China to try to give birth to their babies on Hong Kong soil so that the children qualify for residency rights. Whether this will be the case is unclear.
For Chinese children who enter legally, life is not always easy either. "Sometimes I want to go back to China because I miss my mother," said 12-year-old Fong Kam-mui.
Like many Hong Kong men, Kam-mui's father married a mainland Chinese woman. But Chinese women married to Hong Kong men do not automatically qualify for residency.
Kam-mui is pinning her hopes on the territory's sovereignty change, which she thinks may lead to a shift in policy.
"We'll see if mummy can come after the handover," she said.
In 1995, about 23,000 Chinese children moved to Hong Kong legally to join their parents. The figure for 1996 is not yet available.
